stages.title: Language sounds and pronunciation
stages.hook: Turkish has letters like ı, ö, ü, ş, ç and ğ. Can you guess how a word is said just by reading it?
explain: Turkish spelling is very regular: almost every letter is always said the same way, so you can read a new word aloud with confidence. There are 8 vowels (a, e, ı, i, o, ö, u, ü) and 21 consonants, 29 letters in all.

Some letters need care. The letter ç sounds like ch in chair, ş like sh in ship, and c like j in jam. Dotless ı is a short sound in the back of the mouth, and dotted i is the usual 'ee' sound. The letter ğ is silent; it lengthens the vowel before it. Stress usually falls on the last syllable.
stages.mnemonic: Dots matter: ı is a quiet 'uh', i is a bright 'ee'. Two dots (ö, ü) round your lips like a kiss.

gq.q: How is the Turkish letter ç pronounced?
gq.why: Ç is the 'ch' sound: çay is said 'chai'.

gq.q: Which word contains the dotless ı?
gq.why: Kapı (door) ends in ı, a dotless vowel.

panel.q: A learner reads 'dağ' with a hard g at the end. What is the Turkish rule?
o: The ğ is said like English j
The ğ is silent and lengthens the vowel before it
The ğ is said like k
The ğ is said like h in house
panel.why: Ğ (yumuşak ge, 'soft g') is not pronounced as a consonant; dağ sounds like a long 'daa'.

panel.q: Why can Turkish learners usually read new words aloud easily?
o: Spelling is regular: each letter has one main sound
Words are always spelled like English
panel.why: Turkish adopted the Latin-based alphabet with one sound per letter in 1928.

panel.q: Which pair shows a real vowel difference in Turkish?
panel.why: I (dotless) and i (dotted) are different letters and different sounds; the dot changes the word.

teach.model: Turkish is written the way it is said. Each letter has one main sound. Special letters: ç (ch), ş (sh), ı (dotless), ö and ü (rounded), ğ (silent, lengthens the vowel). Stress is usually on the last syllable.

points.ask: Why is it easy to read?

trip.prompt: Look at the list of letters and find the ones not found in English.

stages.title: Alphabet, script or basic characters
stages.hook: Turkish has a letter with no dot and a letter with a dot, and they are not the same. Why would one dot matter?
explain: The modern Turkish alphabet has 29 letters: a b c ç d e f g ğ h ı i j k l m n o ö p r s ş t u ü v y z. It uses Latin letters and was introduced in 1928. The letters q, w and x are not part of it.

Capital letters follow the dot: ı becomes I and i becomes İ. So 'IŞIK' is capital ışık, and 'İSTANBUL' keeps the dot on its capital İ. Writing İ and I carelessly changes the word. Turkish is written left to right.
stages.mnemonic: Dotless ı gets a plain I; dotted i keeps its dot even as İ.
sentences: The pencil is on the table.

gq.q: What is the capital form of the letter i in Turkish?
gq.why: Dotted i keeps its dot: İstanbul starts with İ.

gq.q: Which letters are NOT in the Turkish alphabet?
gq.why: Turkish has no q, w or x.

panel.q: Someone writes ISTANBUL with a plain I. What does this show?
o: Nothing; I and İ are the same letter
The capital of i should be İ, so İSTANBUL is correct
The word should start with Ş
panel.why: Turkish has two different i letters, each with its own capital.

panel.q: The word 'kâğıt' has a circumflex (â). What does it do?
o: It makes the word a verb
It means the word is foreign
It softens the preceding k and marks a long vowel
panel.why: The circumflex appears in some loanwords to show palatalisation (k sounds like 'ky').

panel.q: Why did the 1928 alphabet reform matter?
o: It replaced the Arabic-based script with a Latin-based one that fits Turkish sounds
It made Turkish right to left
panel.why: The Latin alphabet suited Turkish vowels better and made literacy easier to spread.

teach.model: Turkish has 29 letters in the Latin script. There is no q, w or x. There are two letters i: dotless ı and dotted i. The capitals are I and İ.

trip.prompt: Find the list of 29 letters and spot which English letters are missing.

stages.title: Greetings and introductions
stages.hook: What do you say when you meet someone in Turkey? Do you say the same thing in the morning and the evening?
explain: The common greeting is 'Merhaba' (hello). It works with anyone at any time. 'Selam' is friendlier and more casual. In the morning you say 'Günaydın' (good day, used until noon), later 'İyi günler', and in the evening 'İyi akşamlar'.

To say your name, use 'Benim adım ...' or 'Adım ...' (My name is...). 'Nasılsın?' asks 'How are you?' informally, and 'Nasılsınız?' is formal or plural. A usual answer is 'İyiyim, teşekkürler' (I am fine, thank you). When you leave, you say 'Hoşça kal' to the person staying, or 'Güle güle' to the person leaving.
stages.mnemonic: Merhaba for all, Günaydın for sunrise, Güle güle for a smile on the way out.

gq.q: You are meeting a teacher. Which 'How are you?' is polite?
gq.why: The -nız ending shows respect, so Nasılsınız is used for teachers and elders.

gq.q: Which greeting is used in the morning?

panel.q: A friend leaves your home. What do you say to the person who is leaving?
panel.why: Güle güle ('go smiling') is said to the one leaving; Hoşça kal ('stay well') to the one staying.

panel.q: Why are there two words for 'How are you?' (Nasılsın / Nasılsınız)?
o: One is informal singular, the other is formal or plural
One is only for the past
They are rude and polite for the same person at all times
panel.why: Turkish marks politeness and number in the verb ending.

panel.q: What does the person who says 'Hoşça kal' mean?
o: They are staying and the other person leaves
They are leaving and the other person stays
panel.why: Hoşça kal means 'stay well', so the speaker is the one leaving.

teach.model: Say Merhaba to greet. Use Günaydın in the morning and İyi akşamlar in the evening. To ask 'How are you?' use Nasılsın to a friend and Nasılsınız to a teacher. Say your name with Benim adım ...

points.ask: How do I ask how someone is?
How do I say my name?

trip.prompt: Look for how greetings change with time of day and politeness.

stages.title: Numbers and counting
stages.hook: Count to ten in Turkish. Do you notice any number that sounds like a word you already know?
explain: The numbers from one to ten are bir, iki, üç, dört, beş, altı, yedi, sekiz, dokuz, on. Ten is on. After that, twenty is yirmi, thirty is otuz, forty is kırk, fifty is elli, and a hundred is yüz.

To make 11 you say 'on bir' (ten one), and 21 is 'yirmi bir'. Turkish puts the tens first, then the ones. After a number, the noun stays singular: 'üç kitap' (three book), not a plural. This is a surprise for English speakers!
stages.mnemonic: Bir, iki, üç, dört, beş: count on your hand, and the book stays one.

gq.q: How do you say 'three books' in Turkish?
gq.why: After a number the noun stays singular: üç kitap.
On means 10 and bir means 1, so 'on bir' is 11.

panel.q: Why is 'beş çocuk' correct and 'beş çocuklar' wrong?
o: Turkish nouns stay singular after a number
Numbers above four are not counted
panel.why: The number already shows the plural, so the noun is singular.

panel.q: A shop says 'yirmi iki lira'. What number is this?
panel.why: Yirmi is 20 and iki is 2, so it is 22.

panel.q: Which sequence counts upwards by ones?
panel.why: Dört (4), beş (5), altı (6) is the natural counting order.

teach.model: The numbers are bir, iki, üç, dört, beş, altı, yedi, sekiz, dokuz, on. After a number the noun stays singular, like üç kitap. Eleven is on bir.

points.ask: What happens to the noun after a number?

trip.prompt: Find the table of numbers from 1 to 100.

stages.title: Colours and shapes
stages.hook: Red, blue and green: which one is the colour of the Turkish flag?
explain: Colours in Turkish are adjectives and come before the noun: 'kırmızı elma' (red apple). Common colours are kırmızı (red), mavi (blue), yeşil (green), sarı (yellow), siyah (black), beyaz (white), turuncu (orange) and pembe (pink).

Shapes are daire (circle), kare (square), üçgen (triangle) and dikdörtgen (rectangle). The Turkish flag is red (kırmızı) with a white crescent and star. Adjectives never change for number or gender, so 'kırmızı evler' (red houses) uses the same kırmızı.
stages.mnemonic: The Turkish flag: red kırmızı field, white beyaz moon.

gq.why: The adjective comes before the noun and does not change.

panel.q: How do you say 'red houses'?
panel.why: Adjectives stay the same; only the noun takes the plural -ler.

panel.q: Where does the adjective go in a Turkish noun phrase?
o: At the end of the sentence only
It is attached to the verb
panel.why: Turkish puts adjectives before nouns, like English.

panel.q: A friend says 'üç mavi araba'. What does this show?
o: Number and adjective come before a singular noun
panel.why: The order is number, adjective, noun, with the noun singular.

teach.model: Colours go before the noun: kırmızı elma. They do not change for plural. Shapes are daire (circle), kare (square), üçgen (triangle).

trip.prompt: Find the colours and shapes on the flag.

stages.title: Family and people
stages.hook: Do you call your mother's brother and your father's brother the same word in Turkish?
explain: Family words: anne (mother), baba (father), kardeş (sibling), abla (older sister), abi or ağabey (older brother), dede (grandfather), anneanne (mother's mother) or babaanne (father's mother) (grandmother). Turkish has separate words for the mother's and father's side: dayı (mother's brother), amca (father's brother), teyze (mother's sister), hala (father's sister).

Turkish does not have gender in pronouns: 'o' means he, she or it. So 'O benim annem' is 'She is my mother'. To say 'my', add the ending: anne becomes annem, baba becomes babam. Calling older people 'abla' or 'abi' is also a polite way to talk to someone in the street.
stages.mnemonic: Anne and baba; dayı from mum, amca from dad.

gq.why: Amca is the father's brother; dayı is the mother's brother.

panel.q: Why does Turkish have both amca and dayı?
o: They are two spellings of one word
One is polite, one is rude
It marks which side of the family the uncle is from
panel.why: Turkish kinship words show maternal and paternal sides.

panel.q: Someone says 'O benim kardeşim'. Can you tell if the sibling is a boy or a girl?
o: No, o and kardeş do not show gender
panel.why: Turkish has no grammatical gender, so you need more context.

panel.q: A shop assistant calls an older girl 'abla'. What does this show?
o: It is a respectful, friendly way to address an older girl or woman
It means she is actually a relative
It is a title for teachers only
panel.why: Kinship words are used politely with non-relatives.

teach.model: Anne is mother and baba is father. Use -m for 'my': annem, babam. There are different words for mother's brother (dayı) and father's brother (amca). Turkish o means he, she or it.

points.ask: Why are there different uncle words?

trip.prompt: Compare the words for relatives on the mother's and father's sides.

stages.title: Common objects
stages.hook: Look around you. Can you name five things in Turkish?
explain: Common objects: masa (table), sandalye (chair), kitap (book), kalem (pen or pencil), çanta (bag), kapı (door), pencere (window) and telefon (phone). Turkish uses 'bir' for 'a': 'bir masa' means a table. There is no word for 'the'.

To say 'this is', use 'Bu ...'. To ask what something is, say 'Bu ne?' (What is this?). The answer is 'Bu bir kalem' (This is a pen). The plural ending is -ler or -lar: 'kalemler' (pens), 'çantalar' (bags).
sentences: The books are on the table.

gq.why: After a back vowel (a) the plural is -lar: çantalar.

panel.q: Why is it 'kalemler' but 'çantalar'?
o: The plural vowel follows the last vowel: e takes -ler, a takes -lar
panel.why: Vowel harmony: front vowels take -ler, back vowels take -lar.

panel.q: There is no word for 'the' in Turkish. How do you say 'a book'?
panel.why: Bir means one or a and comes before the noun.

panel.q: You point at an object and ask 'Bu ne?'. Which answer is natural?
panel.why: Bu bir kitap is the natural answer.

teach.model: Say Bu ne? to ask what something is. Answer Bu bir ... Plural uses -ler or -lar depending on the vowel in the word.

points.ask: How do I ask what something is?
How do I make a plural?

trip.prompt: Look at how plural endings change with the last vowel.

stages.title: Everyday actions
stages.hook: How would you say 'I run', 'I eat' and 'I sleep' in Turkish? Where does the verb go?
explain: Turkish verbs end the sentence. The word order is subject, object, verb: 'Ben elma yiyorum' (I apple eat). Everyday verbs are gitmek (to go), gelmek (to come), yemek (to eat), içmek (to drink), uyumak (to sleep) and koşmak (to run).

For 'I am doing', the present continuous adds -yor: 'koşuyorum' (I am running), 'uyuyorum' (I am sleeping). The ending -um shows 'I'. Because the ending shows who does the action, 'ben' (I) is often dropped: 'Yiyorum' alone means 'I am eating'.
stages.mnemonic: The verb always comes last, like the last train.
sentences: I am running in the park.

gq.q: Where does the verb go in a basic Turkish sentence?

gq.why: Uyumak is to sleep; -yorum means 'I am doing'.

panel.q: Why can 'Yiyorum' be a full sentence without 'ben'?
panel.why: The verb ending carries the person, so the pronoun can be dropped.

panel.q: Which order is correct?
panel.why: The verb ends the sentence, with subject and object before it.

panel.q: Which pair is correct for 'I am running'?
panel.why: -um is the 'I' ending; koşuyor would be he or she.

teach.model: The verb goes last: Ben elma yiyorum. For 'I am doing', use -yor plus a personal ending, like koşuyorum. You can drop ben.

points.ask: How do I say 'I am running'?

trip.prompt: Notice that the verb comes at the end of the sentence.

stages.title: Simple listening and speaking
stages.hook: If you hear 'Merhaba, adım Can. Sen kimsin?', what do you answer?
explain: Listen for key words: names after 'adım', questions with 'ne' (what), 'kim' (who), 'nerede' (where), and answers like 'evet' (yes) or 'hayır' (no). Say sounds slowly: Merhaba is mer-ha-BA, with stress on the last syllable.

To speak politely, add 'lütfen' (please) and 'teşekkür ederim' (thank you). 'Anlamadım' means 'I did not understand' and 'Tekrar eder misiniz?' means 'Could you repeat?'. These phrases help when you do not catch what someone says.
stages.mnemonic: Listen for the question word, then answer in the same order.

gq.q: You did not hear a sentence. Which phrase is polite?
gq.why: It politely asks the speaker to repeat.

panel.q: Someone asks 'Nerede?'. What do they want to know?
panel.why: Nerede means where.

panel.q: A friend says 'Adım Can'. How do you reply to introduce yourself?
panel.why: You give your name with 'adım'.

panel.q: Why is 'Anlamadım' useful for a learner?
o: It tells the speaker you did not understand
panel.why: Saying it invites the person to repeat or explain.

teach.model: Listen for question words: kim (who), ne (what), nerede (where). Use Anlamadım if you do not understand and Tekrar eder misiniz? to ask to repeat. Add lütfen to be polite.

points.ask: What if I do not understand?

trip.prompt: Find a few phrases you can use when you do not understand.
